text: Pretty much, Cassini was nearly out of fuel, so the safest parking spot was right into Saturn’s atmosphere. The reason it was not left drifting around a moon is contamination risk. If Cassini had hit Enceladus or Titan, Earth microbes could land there and maybe mess with any native microbial life. Saturn is a giant gassy target, so an unguided collision there is a much cleaner way to retire the probe. It was a planned terminal dive, and it also let science get more data before the spacecraft disintegrated in the hot atmosphere which gave a few final orbits to study Saturn’s clouds.

ok so your stationary leg hurting on a skateboard is super common and it's usually not one single thing, it's the way you're loading that side. when you push with the back leg, the other leg isn't just "stationary" in the sense of doing nothing. it's acting as a counterbalance and absorbing all the wobble from the board, and the ankle, knee and hip all have to stabilize. if you keep your knee a bit stiff or your foot planted too aggressively, the strain builds right up through the shin and hip. a lot of people blame the ankle, but the hip flexors and quads get hammered too because they're working to keep your center of mass over the board.

the most common culprit is a weird push rhythm where you push on that same side way too much, which leaves the other side working overtime just to stay upright. also, people who are new or rusty often land or balance with too much tension in the stationary leg, so the calf and shins get that aching, tired feeling. it's also very possible you're actually overloading the push leg itself: if your pushes are too long and forceful, that side gets tired and starts pulling your stance off balance, and then your non-pushing leg compensates with extra stabilization work. that's the part a lot of riders don't think about.

to reduce the hurt, try making your pushes shorter and more controlled, and don't be so aggressive. switch push sides more often, keep the stationary knee soft and the ankle in a natural, slightly bent position, and focus on letting your body absorb small bumps rather than freezing up. tbh, if you're new to skating, the discomfort is mostly from muscles and joints not used to this kind of constant fine balancing. give your stationary leg a bit more forgiveness, loosen up a touch, and the pain should drop a lot.

I think the term is less about where someone actually lives and more about shared roots. Most Black Americans trace their ancestry to West and Central Africa through the transatlantic slave trade, even if their family has lived in the US for generations and they've never set foot on the continent. 'Afro-American' or 'African American' is a broad label for people of African descent, not a claim that the person came from Africa recently. It became common around the 1960s as part of Black identity movements, to point to the African origin behind many African-American people while distinguishing them from immigrants newly arrived from African countries. It doesn't mean every Black person is from Africa, and it doesn't erase the very different experiences of recent African immigrants and the African-American community. Plenty of Black Americans feel the term fits their heritage, while others prefer 'Black American' or just 'Black'. The key point is that 'African' functions as a geographic/cultural origin marker for African descent, not as a statement that most of them are currently there. So when someone says 'Afro-American,' they're pointing to the diaspora connection, not a passport or current residence. In short, it marks African heritage, not present location.

ok so yeah, I think people frame it like all drugs are bad, and that part gets thrown around a lot. but the deeper question is why the good stuff comes with strings attached, and to me that makes sense biologically rather than morally. pleasure systems do this thing where they build tolerance, so the first dose hits hard and then you need more for that same rush. that's why intensity and 0 adverse effects are in real tension with each other, because strong activation of the reward circuitry often comes with the body and brain adapting. also, the very things that make a drug feel amazing, the dopamine/endorphin surge, the altered perception, can be what makes it dangerous, especially with overuse, dependence, withdrawal or bad interactions. i'm sure there's always an argument that a perfectly tuned substance should exist. i kinda doubt it, not that it's impossible, just that the brain has these negative feedback mechanisms and side effects are often the cost of turning up the volume that much. tbh some milder things can feel pleasant and be safer, and that's why "all drugs are bad" is a bit too broad, because it lumps the gentle stuff in with the intense ones. but for the intense euphoric drugs people usually mean, yeah, there's almost always some adverse effects like sedation, tolerance, dependence risk, or withdrawal. idk, if a drug could deliver a huge reward signal without any price, i'd be surprised if the reward system didn't start compensating. that's a rough way to say it, but imo the body doesn't really let you keep hitting it that hard for free.

thanks for the email. I’m kinda surprised you’re asking this now, but yeah, a few things matter a lot when buying a house. First off, the inspection is where you should actually learn if the place has problems, and you don’t have to accept the seller’s side of things. If the seller won’t share inspection results or fix issues, that’s a red flag. The survey matters too, because it tells you who owns the land, what rights you’ll have, and any restrictions. You also need to be careful with mortgages. Check the terms, ask what happens if rates move, and don’t let pressure make you sign something you haven’t fully read.

I’d also say don’t just look at square footage or the price. Talk to neighbours, check the streets at night, and see how the property feels. Some places look good from the outside but have weird issues inside. And don’t forget the paperwork. You want your title search, insurance, and financing sorted before you go to contract.

one last thing: get someone who actually has your interests in mind, not just whoever is cheapest.

lol I think of it as one formula pretending to be several products. A 3-in-1 body wash/shampoo/conditioner mixes a body cleanser and hair cleaner, with conditioning ingredients in one bottle. That is the main difference from individual products: it uses compromise concentrations so it won't sting your skin or make your hair weird, but it usually does not clean as well as a dedicated body wash or shampoo, and it does not condition as well as a dedicated conditioner. Compared with a 2-in-1 shampoo/conditioner, the extra thing is the body wash side, so it claims to handle skin and hair, while 2-in-1 only covers hair.

For me the tradeoff is lather and performance. A combined formula often makes less foam and leaves some residue when you are not after a deep cleanse. It is convenient for a quick wash, travel, but if you want a very clean scalp or soft hair, the separate products still do a better job. whenever I've used these in a hurry, my hair felt flat afterward, and my skin didn't really smell clean. so I mostly keep the all-in-one for the shower when I can. and tbh it's not bad for now

hey,
good question, and I actually think about this more than I should. They don't watch the whole continent slide in real time, not really. Instead they put up GPS stations on stable ground, then re-measure the same spots again and again over months or years. If a point moves a few cm a year, repeated position data can show that drift in a consistent global reference frame. It's similar to putting markers and checking whether they have inched. I find that bit counterintuitive because continents look totally still to me. They also use satellite geodesy tools like InSAR to watch ground deformation around active margins or fault zones, and VLBI and satellite laser ranging help pin down Earth's orientation and make the global reference frame reliable. So the answer isn't one instrument; it's repeated GPS plus a bunch of geodetic methods that all cross-check each other. For plate speeds, the GPS track data over time is the workhorse, and magnetic striping on the seafloor helps with older spreading rates. The tricky part is separating true plate motion from tiny local ground noise, but with enough repeated measurements the signal comes through. You don't need to be at a fault line to see it.
that's basically how they get numbers for plate motion, not just guess from rocks.

ok so this one sounds simple, but the genetics are a bit messy. inbreeding means close relatives mating, which raises the chance that a child gets two copies of the same harmful mutation. Most people carry a few rare variants that don't cause trouble when masked by a normal copy from the other parent. When relatives share ancestry, those hidden variants are more likely to pair up in the child. IQ is influenced by a lot of genes and environment, so you aren't guaranteed a lower score. The effect is statistical: inbred groups tend to average lower than non-inbred ones, because harmful recessive effects and reduced genetic diversity pull the average down. It's like losing the extra mix that keeps genes robust; fewer combinations means less buffer. I'd be careful with the word caused, because its average, not each kid. Also the environment matters, so we don't blame genetics alone.

this one is worth getting right. a lot of people feel an injury to the arm is not as painful as injuries elsewhere, but that is mostly how the brain sizes up the threat. the arm has less soft tissue and muscle mass than places like the torso or legs, so many hits do not disturb as much. also, an injury in a less vital spot can seem less alarming, which can lower how badly it hurts. that does not mean arm injuries are safe. if a nerve, tendon or bone is involved, the pain can still be severe, and the depth of the wound matters more than the weapon. in other words, a graze is not the same as a fracture or a deep stab, and you should not assume it is minor just because it feels mild. when in doubt, get it looked at by someone who can check for damage.

ok so this one always confused me too, and tbh i get why a new person would mix them up because the names sound nearly identical. pretty much the whole difference comes down to how they stick to the stuff in your blood that carries oxygen. carbon dioxide is a normal waste product of metabolism, and your body deals with it constantly, so you dont even notice it unless the concentration gets absurdly high. it doesn't grab the oxygen carrier the way carbon monoxide does, and it gets converted into bicarbonate in the blood, which makes it easier to handle and remove through breathing.

carbon monoxide is so nasty because it binds to hemoglobin much, much more strongly than oxygen does, kind of like a sticky spot that oxygen has to compete for. once it latches on, it's not going anywhere easily, and that means your tissues don't get enough oxygen. that's what makes it so poisonous when you breathe it in, especially because you don't taste it or smell it, so it can really sneak up on you. and it's not just about oxygen in the blood. CO actually tangles with the enzymes in your cells that use oxygen, which adds to the damage.

co2 only becomes a real problem when there's a ton of it, because it pushes oxygen out of your lungs. but under normal conditions it's just something you exhale all day, so it's not treated like a poison in the same way. i keep coming back to this because i've seen gas detector discussions at work and it clicks once you separate the two: one is a sticky thief for oxygen, the other is normal exhaust your body already knows how to clear. well, not always, because at high enough levels both can suffocate you.

ok so, the brace position is basically how you get your body braced for a hard stop. The crew tells you to tuck your chin and keep your hands low. The point is to keep your head and neck from getting jerked forward or twisted by the impact. In a collision or sudden stop, that's when people get injured the most, so you're trying to make the body act more like a single unit instead of separate parts flying around. It also helps your body stay against the seat and keeps your spine and chest in a safer position. You dont have to make it look perfect, but the idea is to make yourself as protected as possible while you wait for the aircraft to stop. The main thing is that a low, braced position protects the parts of you that get hit first, and keeps you from getting thrown around inside the cabin.

if you're not sure, the basic move is to keep it low and hold on. You're not trying to be a hero, just make yourself less likely to get injured. In an aircraft emergency, it really helps your whole body absorb the stop much better.

pretty much all the companies we know by name had to survive for centuries, and most pre-industrial enterprises were local, family run and often disappeared or got absorbed. A name gets famous when it shows up in more places and eras. Businesses tied to one town or one craft rarely stay in public memory. Trade, wars, technology and changing rules can wipe out long standing names. Some old brands survive because someone kept the name alive, or because they expanded into new markets, but that is not the original business continuing unchanged. Being old is not enough; being known requires surviving decades.

i keep thinking about why a bank can end up cheaper than a dealership, even when the dealer's rate sounds lower. It should be the other way around, but i'm not convinced the low rate wins. The problem is what gets folded into the loan, not just the percentage on the paper.

A dealer can offer 3% and package the loan around a bigger amount: the car's invoice, add-ons, service packages, gap insurance, doc fees. The lower rate then applies to a larger principal. A bank at 5% can still be cheaper if it lends on a cleaner, smaller amount, because the total interest isn't just rate times principal; it's also term length, fees, and penalties.

Let's make it concrete. Say the car's sticker is 30k. If the dealer packages 24k at 3% for 60 months, the rough payment is around 430. If you take a 20k bank loan at 5% for 60 months, it's roughly 378. That's over 50 a month difference, and over five years the gap becomes pretty meaningful. You're not paying for the rate sticker, you're paying for the whole bundle. One thing that catches people off guard is the deposit angle. The 3% rate might only be available after a minimum down payment, or if you buy certain inventory. If the bank's 5% needs no big down payment and a smaller total, it can be cheaper once all costs are added. I ran the numbers once for a friend, and the dealer quote looked better on paper, but the fees and add-ons erased the gap.

There's also fine print. Some dealer deals have prepayment penalties, a short window, or require you to stay in a package you didn't ask for. The bank, at least in my experience, is easier to audit: loan amount, term, fee schedule, early payoff. That transparency changes the calculation.

If I were shopping, I'd take the dealer's low rate as a starting point, then ask a bank to beat it. The bank might not have the flashy 3%, but with a smaller loan and a straightforward payoff schedule, the total cost can be lower. I don't think the rate sticker decides anything by itself. It's an easy mistake to make, because a lower rate feels safe. But safe on paper isn't the same as cheap after fees. I'd also ask what happens if I pay early, and whether add-ons are optional. That question is where real savings usually show up.

Its kinda weird that where marijuana is legal changes state by state, and honestly I think it should just be legal for adults everywhere. Whenever I’ve crossed state lines before, I could feel the rules shift under me, and it makes no sense that what’s allowed in one county can get you in trouble just across the road. My position isn’t that everyone should smoke, but that adults should be able to use and sell it without having to wonder whether they’re doing something illegal. The patchwork is the real problem, especially for people who travel, ship, or visit relatives. If the basics are sorted, then the weird half-measures everywhere else look even messier. I don’t care if states argue about taxes, packaging, or who can open a shop. I just want one clear rule: adults okay, kids not, and don't let state lines make normal life confusing every day.

ok so body electricity is basically ions moving through channels in cell membranes. Nerve cells are like leaky batteries. Sodium floods in, potassium leaks out, and that charge difference is what fires the signal. My heart does it too. The rhythm starts in a tiny bundle of cells that act like a pacemaker. Whenever I move fast or get scared, the signals change speed and strength. Its not magic, just tiny currents doing a lot.

ok so I think the way to think about sampling older songs is to forget that it is some kind of magic. Its just taking a chunk of a record and making it fit what you want to make. whenever I’ve done this, the first thing is actually picking something you genuinely like, not something famous. A melody you keep humming, a bassline you can’t shake, a drum break that just hits different. then you pull the audio in, mark out the exact section, and decide what you need. Maybe you just want four bars of a horn section, or a whole verse looped. You might chop it into slices, reverse bits, stretch it to your tempo, or leave it clean.

What gets people stuck is treating the sample as the final sound. I remember thinking, wait, this is already finished music, why would I put it on top of my own stuff. That mindset makes the track feel like a collage. If you’re gonna use a sample, make it feel like it belongs. That means adjusting the key, maybe filtering out the highs so it sits under your mix, or cutting the sample short so you aren’t fighting yourself for attention. A sample works when it becomes part of your song, not a guest who never leaves.

Also don’t forget the legal stuff because people talk about this and it’s easy to get lazy. A sample is using someone else’s recording, and that usually means clearing it, or using something already in a library where it’s cleared. This is why a lot of people sample from cleared packs, or they work with the original artist or label and split or pay what is required. I’ve seen tracks get pulled or cause drama over this, so take it seriously. But the musical part is the fun bit. You’re not copying the whole song, you’re carving out one small part and using it as a foundation. The best samples feel surprising but also inevitable, like the original artist would recognize their own music in a new setting.

there’s something funny about headaches, because my head feels crushed, but the skull is pretty much not the painful part. The parts that can actually feel pain are the membranes around the brain, the nerves, and the blood vessels. When one of those gets irritated or swells, the trigeminal nerve picks up the signal and sends it to the brain, and that’s the ache you notice. For me it usually starts behind the eye and moves around my temple. I’m often thinking about work, deadlines, or a long screen session, which is when I notice it building up. Dehydration and stress are the usual suspects for me. I’ll usually drink water, lie down, and stop checking emails. I’m not saying every headache is the same, but my position is that most of the time it’s not your head literally breaking. It’s the warning system doing its job, which is annoying but not necessarily bad.

I went to this buffet on a Friday around 4:30 p.m. and, weirdly, there was no line at all. Two people came out to about $130, which felt pretty steep. Before going, I figured the price would be comparable to a steakhouse. Afterward, I learned the buffet actually cost somewhat more than I had expected to pay at one. Honestly, I was disappointed that steak wasn’t offered. At that price, I assumed there would be some kind of steak option. The meat choices included lamb, prime rib, and chicken, but those are things I feel like you can find at other Las Vegas buffets for much less money. The seafood station had Alaskan crab legs and rock crab claws. Alaskan crab legs are available at a lot of Vegas buffets, but I hadn’t run into rock crab claws anywhere else, so those were interesting. The problem was that there were no crab-claw crackers. Staff said wooden mallets were available, but our table was so close to the next table that I didn’t want to start smashing crab shells and send pieces flying at the people next to us. So I just ate the crab legs. The Asian station didn’t seem especially distinctive either. It reminded me quite a bit of the buffet at Rampart Casino. Dessert had gelato and various pastries, but nothing really stood out. They also had fresh juices, although I didn’t try any. I’d call the buffet acceptable, but overpriced for what it offers. If you’re curious, it’s worth trying once, especially if there’s no wait. But if the line is long, I’d probably reconsider.

The space bar rattles. You hit it with the edge of your thumb and it sounds like a loose pen cap rattling in a drawer. The E key also repeats now and then, so "example" comes out as "eexample" and I have to backspace. It happens maybe once an afternoon, always when I'm typing fast and not looking. I paid $38, and I kept it anyway because of the switches. I asked the seller what they were, and the answer took a week. By then I had already pulled off a keycap and found out myself: brown tactile switches, a little bump under the finger and a soft landing at the bottom. My old membrane board felt like pressing wet cardboard by comparison. My work is mostly email, often two or three hours straight, and my wrists don't ache by the end anymore. That mattered more than the rattle. Sending it back would mean paying for postage and boxing it up, and I'd be without a keyboard while waiting. So it stays on the desk, and I do keep tapping the space bar a little closer to the middle now.

yeah I've been to Vegas my whole life, well the under-21 part, so I've seen lots of shows before I could gamble. I finally caught Le Rêve at the Wynn, and honestly it was mixed. Maybe a little worse than mixed.

The good part first: that circular stage is actually pretty smart. You basically look down into it, so from nearly any seat you get a decent view, which is rare in Vegas. A few acts are genuinely impressive, the strength stuff, the aerialists, the divers. Those people are proper athletes, no question. But a lot of it feels like Cirque du Soleil, not in a rip-off way exactly, just that if you've seen Cirque you've already seen comparable moves done with more clarity.

That's really the problem, the clarity. I still don't know what the story is. There's a dream maybe, or a guy, or water. It felt like pretty images thrown at you, and the show never explains what it's going for. Also way too much is happening at once, too many people, too many elements, too many wow moments piled on each other. A more restrained show would hit harder. This felt like the standard Vegas spectacle, where more is better, so they stuffed everything in.

Ticket note: if you stay at Wynn or Encore they have a deal, $99 instead of the usual $125. That helps. Would I go again? Probably not, and I wouldn't pay it a second time. Except for a few stunts it was just average. I wasn't blown away, and I don't think anyone else was either. A few friends did actually like it though, so if you haven't seen it maybe check it out. Just don't walk away expecting to be overwhelmed.

about two years ago we ordered two shirts for my dad from Rockmount Ranch Wear, by phone. The shirts never showed up because the sales rep’s handwriting got read wrong, her 7 became a 1, so 5407 turned into 5401. The people at 5401 took the package to the UPS store for return, and then it just vanished, no update since. We only found out a few weeks later. During the dispute we went ahead and ordered two more shirts. Rockmount wouldn’t refund the first two, and the owner got involved at that point. He admitted the shipment went to the wrong address but said no refund until the shirts came back, and even claimed we’d been not friendly enough to the people at 5401, only four doors away. We disputed the original charge with our credit-card company, and in the end we did get a credit.
